title: My brother sold our family farm while I was in the hospital. When the buyer arrived, he refused to take the keys after seeing my father's name on the barn (PART 2)

blocks.text: Thomas went red. "There's nothing in the root cellar but potatoes and spiders," he said.

Richard walked around to the other side of the barn door and brushed away decades of dust and lichen with his hand. Carved into the wood, smaller, in a different hand, was a second name: S. PRICE 1962.
"Samuel Price was my father," Richard said quietly.

We went to the root cellar together, all of us, even the real estate agent. Behind a stack of old canning jars was a rusted metal box I'd never seen. Thomas wouldn't look at it. Inside was a handwritten partnership agreement, signed by my father and Samuel Price in 1962, witnessed by our family pastor. They had bought the land together, fifty-fifty.
Richard told us the rest. In 1962, his father was a Black farmer in Iowa. No bank in the county would lend to him.

So he and my father, who'd served together in Korea, pooled their savings and bought the farm, putting the deed in my father's name alone because that was the only way to get the mortgage. They farmed it together for six years. In 1968, Samuel moved his family to Minneapolis after their barn was set on fire by people who didn't want them there. He trusted my father to keep his half safe. My father sent Samuel's family a share of the farm's profits every year until he died. Then the payments stopped.
Thomas had found the box when he cleaned out Dad's papers. He hid it. He stopped the payments. And when he needed money, he forged my signature and sold the farm before anyone else could find out.
Richard, now seventy-four, had spent years trying to find out what happened to the land his father talked about until his death.
When the farm came up for sale, he bought it through an agent, hoping to finally stand on it. He never expected to find the agreement.
The sale was voided because of the forgery. Thomas was charged and later pleaded guilty. My share stayed mine.
And then I did what my father would have done. I went to a lawyer and had half of the farm deeded to Richard and his family, as the agreement said.

We farm it together now. My husband and Richard's grandson run the cattle. Richard and I sit on the porch most evenings and trade stories about two young men who came home from a war and decided to be partners when the world told them they couldn't.
Last summer, we replaced the old barn door. We kept both carvings. We added a third line underneath: PARTNERS 1962. STILL.
